claim: cAMP regulates gene transcription principally by activating the protein kinase A (PKA)-targeted transcription factors.
source: It is widely accepted that cAMP regulates gene transcription principally by activating the protein kinase A (PKA)-targeted transcription factors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: cAMP enhances the generation of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) in multiple cell types.
source: Here, we show that cAMP enhances the generation of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) in multiple cell types.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: 5hmC is converted from 5-methylcytosine (5mC) by Tet methylcytosine dioxygenases.
source: 5hmC is converted from 5-methylcytosine (5mC) by Tet methylcytosine dioxygenases, for which Fe(II) is an essential cofactor.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Tet enzyme function.

claim: Fe(II) is an essential cofactor for Tet methylcytosine dioxygenases.
source: 5hmC is converted from 5-methylcytosine (5mC) by Tet methylcytosine dioxygenases, for which Fe(II) is an essential cofactor.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Tet enzyme cofactor requirements.

claim: The promotion of 5hmC by cAMP was mediated by a prompt increase of the intracellular labile Fe(II) pool (LIP).
source: The promotion of 5hmC was mediated by a prompt increase of the intracellular labile Fe(II) pool (LIP).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: cAMP enhanced the acidification of endosomes for Fe(II) release to the LIP likely through RapGEF2.
source: cAMP enhanced the acidification of endosomes for Fe(II) release to the LIP likely through RapGEF2.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract with speculative language ('likely') supported by experimental data.

claim: The effect of cAMP on Fe(II) and 5hmC was confirmed by adenylate cyclase activators.
source: The effect of cAMP on Fe(II) and 5hmC was confirmed by adenylate cyclase activators, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, and most notably by stimulation of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of cAMP on Fe(II) and 5hmC was confirmed by phosphodiesterase inhibitors.
source: The effect of cAMP on Fe(II) and 5hmC was confirmed by adenylate cyclase activators, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, and most notably by stimulation of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of cAMP on Fe(II) and 5hmC was confirmed by stimulation of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR).
source: The effect of cAMP on Fe(II) and 5hmC was confirmed by adenylate cyclase activators, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, and most notably by stimulation of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The transcriptomic changes caused by cAMP occurred in concert with 5hmC elevation in differentially transcribed genes.
source: The transcriptomic changes caused by cAMP occurred in concert with 5hmC elevation in differentially transcribed genes.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq and hMeDIP-seq data.

claim: GPCR-cAMP signaling regulates gene transcription through augmentation of the intracellular labile Fe(II) pool and DNA hydroxymethylation.
source: Collectively, these data show a previously unrecognized regulation of gene transcription by GPCR-cAMP signaling through augmentation of the intracellular labile Fe(II) pool and DNA hydroxymethylation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: cAMP exerts its function through three major targets: cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA), cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channels (CNGCs), and exchange protein directly activated by cAMP (Epac).
source: Principally, cAMP exerts its function through three major targets − cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA), cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channels (CNGCs), and exchange protein directly activated by cAMP (Epac).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cAMP signaling pathways.

claim: cAMP has an impact on gene transcription, which is currently considered to be mediated by the PKA-targeted transcription factors.
source: It is well known that cAMP has an impact on gene transcription, which is currently considered to be mediated by the PKA-targeted transcription factors (Montminy, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Three transcription factors, including cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), cAMP response element modulator (CREM), and activating transcription factor 1 (ATF1), can be phosphorylated by PKA.
source: Three transcription factors, including cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), cAMP response element modulator (CREM), and activating transcription factor 1 (ATF1), can be phosphorylated by PKA and subsequently bind to cAMP response elements (CRE) in gene promoters, generally to activate gene transcription (Sands and Palmer, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CREB, CREM, and ATF1 subsequently bind to cAMP response elements (CRE) in gene promoters after phosphorylation by PKA.
source: Three transcription factors, including cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), cAMP response element modulator (CREM), and activating transcription factor 1 (ATF1), can be phosphorylated by PKA and subsequently bind to cAMP response elements (CRE) in gene promoters, generally to activate gene transcription (Sands and Palmer, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Schwann cells form the myelin sheath of axons within the peripheral nervous system.
source: Schwann cells form the myelin sheath of axons within the peripheral nervous system.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: cAMP is a known instructive signal for Schwann cell differentiation into a myelinating phenotype.
source: cAMP is a known instructive signal for Schwann cell differentiation into a myelinating phenotype (Jessen et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: cAMP directly induces cell cycle arrest in Schwann cells.
source: cAMP directly induces cell cycle arrest along with the expression of a wide variety of myelination-associated genes such as Egr2/Krox20, a transcription factor that is considered a master regulator of the myelin program, and myelin protein zero, the main peripheral nerve myelin protein (Bacallao and Monje, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: cAMP induces the expression of myelination-associated genes such as Egr2/Krox20 in Schwann cells.
source: cAMP directly induces cell cycle arrest along with the expression of a wide variety of myelination-associated genes such as Egr2/Krox20, a transcription factor that is considered a master regulator of the myelin program, and myelin protein zero, the main peripheral nerve myelin protein (Bacallao and Monje, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Egr2/Krox20 is considered a master regulator of the myelin program.
source: cAMP directly induces cell cycle arrest along with the expression of a wide variety of myelination-associated genes such as Egr2/Krox20, a transcription factor that is considered a master regulator of the myelin program, and myelin protein zero, the main peripheral nerve myelin protein (Bacallao and Monje, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Myelin protein zero is the main peripheral nerve myelin protein.
source: cAMP directly induces cell cycle arrest along with the expression of a wide variety of myelination-associated genes such as Egr2/Krox20, a transcription factor that is considered a master regulator of the myelin program, and myelin protein zero, the main peripheral nerve myelin protein (Bacallao and Monje, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The mechanism by which cAMP regulates transcription and promotes the differentiation of Schwann cells is not fully understood.
source: However, the mechanism by which cAMP regulates transcription and promotes the differentiation of Schwann cells is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Active DNA demethylation is catalyzed by ten-eleven translocation (Tet) methylcytosine dioxygenases.
source: Active DNA demethylation is catalyzed by ten-eleven translocation (Tet) methylcytosine dioxygenases, which oxidize 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) (Tahiliani et al., 2009; Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009), and further to 5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC) (He et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Tet methylcytosine dioxygenases oxidize 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC).
source: Active DNA demethylation is catalyzed by ten-eleven translocation (Tet) methylcytosine dioxygenases, which oxidize 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) (Tahiliani et al., 2009; Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009), and further to 5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC) (He et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Tet methylcytosine dioxygenases oxidize 5hmC further to 5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC).
source: Active DNA demethylation is catalyzed by ten-eleven translocation (Tet) methylcytosine dioxygenases, which oxidize 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) (Tahiliani et al., 2009; Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009), and further to 5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC) (He et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: 5fC and 5caC are ultimately replaced by unmodified cytosine (5C) to complete cytosine demethylation.
source: 5fC and 5caC are ultimately replaced by unmodified cytosine (5C) to complete cytosine demethylation (Pastor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: 5hmC is a unique epigenetic mark with regulatory capacities in addition to being a DNA demethylation intermediate.
source: It is noteworthy that 5hmC is also a unique epigenetic mark with regulatory capacities in addition to being a DNA demethylation intermediate (Shen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Tet belongs to the iron and 2-oxoglutarate (2OG)-dependent dioxygenase family.
source: Tet belongs to the iron and 2-oxoglutarate (2OG, alternatively known as α-ketoglutarate)-dependent dioxygenase family which utilizes labile Fe(II) as a cofactor and 2OG as a co-substrate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzyme family.

claim: Tet utilizes labile Fe(II) as a cofactor and 2OG as a co-substrate.
source: Tet belongs to the iron and 2-oxoglutarate (2OG, alternatively known as α-ketoglutarate)-dependent dioxygenase family which utilizes labile Fe(II) as a cofactor and 2OG as a co-substrate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Tet enzyme requirements.

claim: Ascorbate has the capacity to reduce the redox-inactive Fe(III)/Fe(IV) to Fe(II).
source: We and others have shown that ascorbate, which has the capacity to reduce the redox-inactive Fe(III)/Fe(IV) to Fe(II), is another cofactor for Tet (Minor et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2013; Blaschke et al., 2013; Dickson et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ascorbate is a cofactor for Tet.
source: We and others have shown that ascorbate, which has the capacity to reduce the redox-inactive Fe(III)/Fe(IV) to Fe(II), is another cofactor for Tet (Minor et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2013; Blaschke et al., 2013; Dickson et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ascorbate has an impact on DNA demethylation by promoting the availability of redox-active Fe(II) to Tet.
source: Thus, ascorbate has an impact on DNA demethylation by promoting the availability of redox-active Fe(II) to Tet.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about ascorbate and Tet.

claim: Ascorbate was identified as an essential factor for Schwann cells to initiate and promote myelin formation.
source: Similar to cAMP, ascorbate was identified as another essential factor for Schwann cells to initiate and promote myelin formation (Bunge et al., 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Intracellular ascorbate deficiency can cause hypomyelination in modeled rodents.
source: Intracellular ascorbate deficiency can cause hypomyelination in modeled rodents (Gess et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Treatment with ascorbate (50 μM) for 3 days induced 5hmC in Schwann cells.
source: Dot-blot shows that treatment with ascorbate (50 μM) for 3 days or cAMP (100 μM) for 7 days induced 5hmC in Schwann cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the figure legend.

claim: Treatment with cAMP (100 μM) for 7 days induced 5hmC in Schwann cells.
source: Dot-blot shows that treatment with ascorbate (50 μM) for 3 days or cAMP (100 μM) for 7 days induced 5hmC in Schwann cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the figure legend.

claim: In the absence of cAMP treatment, 5hmC was barely detectable by dot blot in primary cultured rat Schwann cells.
source: In the absence of cAMP treatment, 5hmC was barely detectable by dot blot in primary cultured rat Schwann cells.
evidence: This is an experimental observation reported in the Results section.

claim: After treatment with membrane-permeable 8-CPT-cAMP (100 μM), 5hmC signal emerged at comparable levels to cells treated with ascorbate (50 μM).
source: However, after treatment with membrane-permeable 8-CPT-cAMP (hereafter denoted as cAMP) (100 μM), 5hmC signal emerged at comparable levels to cells treated with ascorbate (50 μM, Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1A and B.

claim: The addition of cAMP (0–250 μM) dose-dependently increased 5hmC generation in Schwann cells.
source: The addition of cAMP (0–250 μM) dose-dependently increased 5hmC generation in Schwann cells (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1C and D.

claim: The IF signal for 5hmC was sustained for 1–7 days upon continuous cAMP (100 μM) treatment.
source: The IF signal for 5hmC was sustained for 1–7 days upon continuous cAMP (100 μM) treatment (Figure 1E and F), suggesting that continuous cAMP treatment largely maintained 5hmC.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1E and F.

claim: Continuous cAMP treatment largely maintained 5hmC.
source: The IF signal for 5hmC was sustained for 1–7 days upon continuous cAMP (100 μM) treatment (Figure 1E and F), suggesting that continuous cAMP treatment largely maintained 5hmC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sustained IF signal data.

claim: An enhanced generation of 5hmC was verified in HEK-293 cells, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) and neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells.
source: An enhanced generation of 5hmC was also verified in other cell types examined, such as HEK-293 cells, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) and neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells, indicating that the effect of cAMP on 5hmC is not limited to Schwann cells and is likely to be a general effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of cAMP on 5hmC is not limited to Schwann cells and is likely to be a general effect.
source: An enhanced generation of 5hmC was also verified in other cell types examined, such as HEK-293 cells, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) and neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells, indicating that the effect of cAMP on 5hmC is not limited to Schwann cells and is likely to be a general effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations in multiple cell types.

claim: Treatment with AMP (100 μM) for 2 days did not induce 5hmC in Schwann cells.
source: AMP (100 μM) treatment for 2 days did not induce 5hmC while AC activators (forskolin (100 μM), bicarbonate (50 mM)), and PDE inhibitors (caffeine (100 μM), IBMX (100 μM)) enhanced 5hmC generation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: AC activators (forskolin (100 μM), bicarbonate (50 mM)) enhanced 5hmC generation in Schwann cells.
source: AMP (100 μM) treatment for 2 days did not induce 5hmC while AC activators (forskolin (100 μM), bicarbonate (50 mM)), and PDE inhibitors (caffeine (100 μM), IBMX (100 μM)) enhanced 5hmC generation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: PDE inhibitors (caffeine (100 μM), IBMX (100 μM)) enhanced 5hmC generation in Schwann cells.
source: AMP (100 μM) treatment for 2 days did not induce 5hmC while AC activators (forskolin (100 μM), bicarbonate (50 mM)), and PDE inhibitors (caffeine (100 μM), IBMX (100 μM)) enhanced 5hmC generation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Treating cells with forskolin, which directly activates transmembrane adenylate cyclase (AC) to produce endogenous cAMP, promoted 5hmC generation in Schwann cells.
source: Treating cells with forskolin, which directly activates transmembrane adenylate cyclase (AC) to produce endogenous cAMP, promoted 5hmC generation in Schwann cells as did bicarbonate, an activator of soluble AC (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1G and H.

claim: Bicarbonate is an activator of soluble AC.
source: Treating cells with forskolin, which directly activates transmembrane adenylate cyclase (AC) to produce endogenous cAMP, promoted 5hmC generation in Schwann cells as did bicarbonate, an activator of soluble AC (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bicarbonate's function.

claim: Bicarbonate promoted 5hmC generation in Schwann cells.
source: Treating cells with forskolin, which directly activates transmembrane adenylate cyclase (AC) to produce endogenous cAMP, promoted 5hmC generation in Schwann cells as did bicarbonate, an activator of soluble AC (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1G and H.

claim: The production of 5hmC was observed when cells were treated with phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitors caffeine or IBMX.
source: The production of 5hmC was also observed when cells were treated with phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitors caffeine or IBMX, both of which prevent cAMP degradation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Caffeine and IBMX prevent cAMP degradation.
source: The production of 5hmC was also observed when cells were treated with phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitors caffeine or IBMX, both of which prevent cAMP degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PDE inhibitor function.

claim: No 5hmC signal was observed after cells were treated with AMP (100 μM).
source: Conversely, no 5hmC signal was observed after cells were treated with AMP (100 μM).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Endogenous cAMP is involved in 5hmC generation.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that endogenous cAMP is indeed involved in 5hmC generation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of AC activators and PDE inhibitors.

claim: Treatment of Schwann cells with forskolin (10 μM) for 3 hr followed by washout induced 5hmC elevation at 24 or 72 hr time points comparable to continuous treatment.
source: To test whether the long-term effect on 5hmC relies on the continuous presence of cAMP or forskolin in the media, we treated Schwann cells with forskolin (10 μM) for 3–24 hr followed by washout. An increase of 5hmC was detected at both 24 or 72 hr time points, which is comparable to continuous treatment for 24 or 72 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Shorter treatments (1–4 hr) with cAMP (10 μM) or forskolin (10 μM) followed by washout induced 5hmC elevation at levels comparable to continuous treatment for 24 hr in HEK-293 cells.
source: Shorter treatments (1–4 hr) with cAMP (10 μM) or forskolin (10 μM) followed by washout also induced 5hmC elevation at levels comparable to continuous treatment for 24 hr in HEK-293 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: 5hmC level appeared to retreat toward the base line at the 72 hr time point in the fast replicating HEK-293 cells.
source: However, unlike in Schwann cells, 5hmC level appeared to retreat toward the base line at the 72 hr time point in the fast replicating HEK-293 cells.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: 5hmC is not maintained during DNA synthesis.
source: Since 5hmC is not maintained during DNA synthesis, it is thus reasonable that 5hmC could be kept longer in the slowly dividing Schwann cells after termination of cAMP signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about 5hmC behavior during DNA replication.

claim: 5hmC could be kept longer in the slowly dividing Schwann cells after termination of cAMP signaling.
source: Since 5hmC is not maintained during DNA synthesis, it is thus reasonable that 5hmC could be kept longer in the slowly dividing Schwann cells after termination of cAMP signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knowledge that 5hmC is not maintained during DNA synthesis.

claim: cAMP can produce a persistent increase in 5hmC, which can be detected within a few hours after treatment and last for several days depending on cell types.
source: These experiments suggest that cAMP can produce a persistent increase in 5hmC, which can be detected within a few hours after treatment and last for several days depending on cell types.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations.

claim: mRNA levels of Tet2 and Tet3 were decreased after treatment with cAMP (100 μM) for 1 day.
source: mRNA levels of Tet2 and Tet3 were decreased, whereas Tet1 mRNA remained unchanged after treatment with cAMP (100 μM) for 1 day (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and Figure 1—source data 1), a time point at which cAMP clearly promoted 5hmC generation (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Tet1 mRNA remained unchanged after treatment with cAMP (100 μM) for 1 day.
source: mRNA levels of Tet2 and Tet3 were decreased, whereas Tet1 mRNA remained unchanged after treatment with cAMP (100 μM) for 1 day (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and Figure 1—source data 1), a time point at which cAMP clearly promoted 5hmC generation (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The increased level of 5hmC does not appear to be mediated by an effect of cAMP on the expression of Tet.
source: Thus, the increased level of 5hmC does not appear to be mediated by an effect of cAMP on the expression of Tet.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Tet expression decreased or remained unchanged while 5hmC increased.

claim: In healthy cells such as primary cultured Schwann cells, the most plausible rate-limiting factor for Tet's enzymatic activity is the replenishment of the Fe(II) cofactor rather than 2OG.
source: In healthy cells such as primary cultured Schwann cells, the most plausible rate-limiting factor for Tet's enzymatic activity is the replenishment of the Fe(II) cofactor rather than 2OG, a relatively abundant intermediate of the Krebs cycle.
evidence: This is a speculation based on knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: 2OG is a relatively abundant intermediate of the Krebs cycle.
source: In healthy cells such as primary cultured Schwann cells, the most plausible rate-limiting factor for Tet's enzymatic activity is the replenishment of the Fe(II) cofactor rather than 2OG, a relatively abundant intermediate of the Krebs cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: Treatment with cAMP at a dose as low as 1 μM increased intracellular labile Fe(II).
source: Treatment with cAMP at a dose as low as 1 μM increased intracellular labile Fe(II), which reached even higher levels after treatment with 10–100 μM cAMP (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2A and B.

claim: Intracellular labile Fe(II) reached even higher levels after treatment with 10–100 μM cAMP.
source: Treatment with cAMP at a dose as low as 1 μM increased intracellular labile Fe(II), which reached even higher levels after treatment with 10–100 μM cAMP (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2A and B.

claim: Incubation of the cells with Diox-Puro showed no IF signal after cAMP treatment indicating the Fe(II) dependence of the signal detected by Trx-Puro.
source: Incubation of the cells with Diox-Puro (Spangler et al., 2016), a dioxolane control conjugate that is non-peroxidic, showed no IF signal after cAMP treatment indicating the Fe(II) dependence of the signal detected by Trx-Puro (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The action of cAMP on intracellular labile Fe(II) was rapid.
source: The action of cAMP on intracellular labile Fe(II) was rapid. Fe(II) signal appeared within 2 hr (the minimal time for simultaneous incubation of cAMP and Trx-Puro) and peaked at 4 hr after cAMP treatment (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2C and D.

claim: Fe(II) signal appeared within 2 hr and peaked at 4 hr after cAMP treatment.
source: The action of cAMP on intracellular labile Fe(II) was rapid. Fe(II) signal appeared within 2 hr (the minimal time for simultaneous incubation of cAMP and Trx-Puro) and peaked at 4 hr after cAMP treatment (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2C and D.

claim: The effect of cAMP on intracellular labile Fe(II) was validated in HEK-293, MEF, and SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Similar to 5hmC, the effect of cAMP on intracellular labile Fe(II) was also validated in other types of cells including HEK-293, MEF, and SH-SY5Y (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that it is likely a general effect.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effect of cAMP on intracellular labile Fe(II) is likely a general effect.
source: Similar to 5hmC, the effect of cAMP on intracellular labile Fe(II) was also validated in other types of cells including HEK-293, MEF, and SH-SY5Y (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that it is likely a general effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations in multiple cell types.

claim: A significant increase of labile Fe(II) was detected in cells after treatments with cAMP (10, 100 μM) for 4 hr using the FIP-1 probe.
source: Using the FIP-1 probe, a significant increase of labile Fe(II) was detected in cells after treatments with cAMP (10, 100 μM) for 4 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: cAMP treatment likely elevated labile Fe(II) in the cell.
source: Taken together, the results from two different independent chemical methods verified that cAMP treatment likely elevated labile Fe(II) in the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from two independent methods.

claim: Treatment with AMP had no observable effect on labile Fe(II).
source: Treatment with AMP had no observable effect on labile Fe(II).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Elevating endogenous cAMP augmented intracellular labile Fe(II), as demonstrated by the treatment of Schwann cells with AC activators (forskolin, bicarbonate) and PDE inhibitors (caffeine, IBMX).
source: Elevating endogenous cAMP also augmented intracellular labile Fe(II), as demonstrated by the treatment of Schwann cells with AC activators (forskolin, bicarbonate) and PDE inhibitors (caffeine, IBMX) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3A and B.

claim: Treatment of Schwann cells with forskolin (10 μM) for 3 hr followed by washout showed that labile Fe(II) immediately increased after the treatment but quickly declined back to the baseline levels after another 3 hr.
source: To further examine the time course of labile iron response to cAMP, we treated Schwann cells with forskolin (10 μM) for 3 hr followed by washout. Labile Fe(II) immediately increased after the treatment but quickly declined back to the baseline levels after another 3 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of cAMP on labile Fe(II) elevation is relatively transient.
source: These results suggest that the effect of cAMP on labile Fe(II) elevation is relatively transient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid decline of labile Fe(II) after forskolin washout.

claim: Intracellular labile Fe(II) might be tightly controlled within the cell and therefore any increase in the LIP would not last a long time.
source: Alternatively, intracellular labile Fe(II) might be tightly controlled within the cell and therefore any increase in the LIP would not last a long time.
evidence: This is a speculation about cellular iron regulation.

claim: Ascorbate at physiological levels has no obvious influence on intracellular labile Fe(II).
source: Ascorbate at physiological levels has been shown to have no obvious influence on intracellular labile Fe(II) (Spangler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: No obvious change in the intracellular labile Fe(II) pool was observed in Schwann cells after treatment with ascorbate at a physiological concentration (50 μM).
source: Indeed, no obvious change in the intracellular labile Fe(II) pool was observed in Schwann cells after treatment with ascorbate at a physiological concentration (50 μM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that ascorbate may only increase the bioavailability of Fe(II) to Tet and other enzymes locally.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ascorbate may only increase the bioavailability of Fe(II) to Tet and other enzymes locally.
source: Indeed, no obvious change in the intracellular labile Fe(II) pool was observed in Schwann cells after treatment with ascorbate at a physiological concentration (50 μM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that ascorbate may only increase the bioavailability of Fe(II) to Tet and other enzymes locally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of global Fe(II) change with ascorbate treatment.

claim: Iron chelators 2,2, bipyridyl (20 μM) and deferoxamine (20 μM) drastically decreased the level of labile Fe(II).
source: To determine whether cAMP promotes 5hmC generation via labile Fe(II), Schwann cells were treated with two different iron chelators 2,2, bipyridyl (20 μM) and deferoxamine (20 μM) prior to cAMP stimulation. These iron chelators drastically decreased the level of labile Fe(II) and further abolished the effect of cAMP on 5hmC in Schwann cells (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3C and D.

claim: Iron chelators abolished the effect of cAMP on 5hmC in Schwann cells.
source: To determine whether cAMP promotes 5hmC generation via labile Fe(II), Schwann cells were treated with two different iron chelators 2,2, bipyridyl (20 μM) and deferoxamine (20 μM) prior to cAMP stimulation. These iron chelators drastically decreased the level of labile Fe(II) and further abolished the effect of cAMP on 5hmC in Schwann cells (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3C and D.

claim: The abolishing effect of the iron chelators on cAMP-induced 5hmC generation was verified in human melanoma A2058 cells.
source: The abolishing effect of the iron chelators on cAMP-induced 5hmC generation was also verified in other cells such as human melanoma A2058 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: cAMP upregulates 5hmC by elevating intracellular labile Fe(II).
